sections.h: The call and first sign acts
sections.b: Ezekiel is called by the Kebar canal in 593 BC (Ezekiel 1:1-3:15), made a watchman (Ezekiel 3:16-21) and then shut in and made mute (Ezekiel 3:22-27). In chapters 4 to 7 he acts out the siege of Jerusalem, lies on his side for the guilt of Israel and Judah, shaves and divides his hair, and speaks to the mountains of Israel and to the land.

In Ezekiel 1 the glory of the LORD appears to a priest among the exiles, on a throne carried by living creatures. He is the God who travels. The same glory stands before him on the plain (Ezekiel 3:23) and will later leave the Temple (Ezekiel 10) and return to the new one (Ezekiel 43).

Ezekiel's living creatures have four faces, a human, a lion, an ox and an eagle, four wings and straight legs. They carry the dome and the throne, with a wheel at each. Chapter 10 names them cherubim, and the face of the ox is called a cherub's face there.

Ezekiel does not call the living creatures of chapter 1 cherubim; he only says so in chapter 10. Both chapters describe a mobile throne carried by winged beings, in the image of the cherubim over the ark in the Temple.

The blue throne above the dome is the LORD's seat, carried by living creatures and wheels. It is not in Jerusalem, but with the exiles. Its shape recalls the sapphire pavement under God's feet in Exodus 24:10 and the throne rooms of ancient kings.

God calls Ezekiel ben adam, 'son of man', 93 times in the book, first in Ezekiel 2:1. In Hebrew it is a plain word for a human being. Rashi gives two reasons: it reminds a man who has seen the Chariot that he is human, and it keeps him from pride (reported from Sefaria). The Gospel title is a separate question.

Ezekiel is made a watchman for the house of Israel (Ezekiel 3:17). If he warns, he saves himself even if the hearer does not listen; if he stays silent, he is answerable for the blood of the one who dies. The picture is also used by other prophets, and Paul uses similar words in Acts.

sections.b: In chapters 4 and 5 Ezekiel lies on his side for 390 and 40 days, eats rationed bread baked on dung and divides his shaved hair in thirds. Each act is a message to the exiles about the siege of Jerusalem. Other prophets also acted out messages.

Ezekiel lived at Tel-abib on the Kebar canal among the Judeans deported in 597 BC. The exiles hear him, but do not obey. His first message is that the exile will not be short and the siege of Jerusalem will happen.

Ezekiel's own word for idols, gillulim, is a mocking term close to the word for dung pellets. In chapters 6 and 7 the slain will lie among them, and silver and gold will turn to filth. Ezekiel also uses shiqqutsim, detestable things, and to'evot, abhorrent things.

Ezekiel says that the high places, the local altars on hills and under trees, are still in use and will be destroyed by the sword. The old command to destroy them is in Leviticus 26:30 and Deuteronomy 12:2-3.

In Ezekiel 6:8-10 the LORD leaves some alive, scattered among the nations. They will remember him and be disgusted with themselves. Later chapters turn this remnant to hope (Ezekiel 11:16-21; Ezekiel 36).

sections.h: Jerusalem in the middle of the nations
sections.b: Ezekiel 5:5 says that Jerusalem stands in the middle of the nations, so that its failure is seen by all. The chapter then describes siege, famine, plague and exile, in the language of the covenant curses.
Chapters 4 to 6 repeat the curses of Leviticus 26: bread by weight, the staff of bread, wild animals, sword, plague, eating children, the high places cut down, corpses on idols and the scattering.

Ezekiel is a priest and a prophet. His call includes a scroll to eat, a watchman's duty and a mouth that opens only when God speaks. His sign acts and oracles show that a prophet can be called to suffer the message he brings.
